quick.summary: How to stop fixing the same data problem every week.
quick.takeaway: Stop treating the symptom. Ask why until you find the true cause.

beats.line: Our dashboard breaks every Friday. I patch it, but it keeps happening. Why?
You are mopping the floor while the sink is still overflowing.
I have to mop the floor, or people slip.
True. But you also need to turn off the tap.
We must separate the symptom from the cause.
The industry calls this root cause analysis.
Can I just say find the leak?
That works. Find the leak.
The broken dashboard is water on the floor. How do I find the tap?
You become a toddler. You just keep asking why.
Why did the dashboard break? Because the table was locked.
Good. Why was the table locked?
Because a massive batch job runs at the same time.
Why does the job run then?
Because the finance team set it up that way years ago.
There is your tap.
So I move the batch job to midnight, and the dashboard stops breaking.
You fixed the cause, not just the symptom.
I am going to put the mop away now.
Enjoy your dry floor.

quiz.question: What is the best way to stop a recurring data error?
options: Keep asking why until you discover the original source of the failure.
Write a script that automatically applies a patch every time it breaks.
Ignore the problem until the business decides to replace the system.
Assign a dedicated engineer to fix it manually each week.
quiz.explanation: If you only patch the symptom, the problem will return. You must trace the error back to its source.

quiz.question: Fixing the symptom is a permanent solution to a problem.
quiz.explanation: Fixing the symptom is like mopping up a spill without fixing the leak. The problem will always come back.
